note: Script read on a call, in English. far = the team lead, mic = the candidate (profile en-technical-backend). Sentences are scored independently, so extra speech between them is free. Read them in order, far then mic.
far: Thanks for joining. I wrote the original billing service, so I will be asking about it. Tell me about a system you replaced without a big bang rewrite
How did you decide the new engine was safe to switch to
What did you do when the two engines disagreed
Our billing tables are write heavy. What happens to a Postgres query under that kind of load
How would you find out that autovacuum is falling behind
Let's say we want to move an endpoint to a new service. How do you do that without downtime
What if a client retries a payment request during the cutover
We have two junior engineers joining the team. How do you mentor them
What do you do when a junior engineer's pull request is wrong in a way that matters
Do you have any questions for me
mic: At Arbor Systems we replaced a fourteen year old pricing engine. We did not rewrite it in one go. We ran both engines in parallel against live traffic for six weeks
We compared the outputs every night and defined an error budget up front. We switched when the residual difference held under 0.05 percent
Every disagreement became a ticket with the input that caused it. Most were rounding rules nobody had written down, and we added tests for each one before changing anything

Writers and readers contend for the same pages, so latency grows with lock waits and with dead tuples that vacuum has not cleaned yet. Indexes make writes slower too, so I would check which ones are really used
I would watch dead tuples per table and the age of the oldest transaction, and compare vacuum duration to the rate of updates. A long running transaction blocks cleanup for everyone
Put the new service behind a feature flag, send a small share of traffic, and keep the old path as the fallback. Roll forward only while the error rate stays inside the budget
The payment request needs an idempotency key, stored with the result, so a retry returns the first answer instead of charging twice. That has to exist before the cutover starts, not after
I pair with them on the first few changes and explain why, not only what. Then I review their work for the reasoning, and I let them make small mistakes in a safe place
I say what the risk is, with a concrete failing case, and ask them how they would fix it. If they find it themselves they keep it
Yes. What does on-call actually look like for the platform team, and how often does a person get paged
